newsitem.title: UK: Zinc's bullish fundamentals seen heating up prices.
newsitem.headline: Zinc's bullish fundamentals seen heating up prices.

text.p: Zinc prices, up this week at 10-month highs, have the potential to add several hundred dollars more in 1997 as stocks erode and demand exceeds supply.
But metals analysts add that the rally, which has been led by fund buyers, could meet resistance from selling out of China. China already produces a surplus and may expand its output.
Three month zinc prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME) soared on Tuesday to $1,113 for a gain of $43 or four percent, spurred by a big draw on stocks.
Prices, which were holding on Wednesday around Tuesday's highs, are up about 12 percent from last year's low of $997.

"The zinc outlook is very promising," said analyst Robin Bahr of broker Brandeis. "Whereas the outlook for the others is ambivalent at best, certainly for zinc it does look like a pretty good one-way bet."
Eighteen metals analysts polled by Reuters last week forecast an average zinc cash price in 1997 of 53.9 cents per lb ($1,188 per tonne), up from 46.5 cents/lb ($1,025) last year.
Bahr sees three month zinc prices peaking at $1,300 to $1,350 in the fourth quarter of 1997.
Forecasters expect LME supervised zinc stocks to continue falling after an 11,975-tonne decline on Tuesday, which brought total exchange stocks down to their lowest in four years.
"LME zinc stocks have now recorded 29 consecutive month-on-month drawdowns," said Nick Moore, analyst with Flemings Global Mining Group.
Stocks have dropped by 61 percent since October 18, 1994 when they peaked at 1.24 million tonnes, he added.
"What may surprise you is that the zinc price at the time of the all-time stock peak was 47.8 cents per lb, about the same as it is now," Moore added in a commentary.
If stocks continue to fall at rate of 19,000 tonnes a month as they have over the last three months, inventories will hit critical levels in 13 months, Moore added.
As stocks fall, the production side has been starved of investment due to low prices and over the past six months zinc mines have announced a series of cutbacks and closures.
"European smelters may have to restrain production because they cannot get material," Bahr said.
But China produces each year about 100-200,000 tonnes over domestic consumption, which is available for export, he said.
China's capacity was cited this week by broker GNI Ltd in its commodities Outlook 1997.
GNI also took a less bullish view of zinc than several other analysts, citing factors that included China.
"The country's production potential will be enormous over the next few years," GNI said.
China's smelting capacity is seen rising from 1.07 million tonnes per year at end-1995 to 1.46 million at the end of this year and 1.58 million by the turn of the century, GNI said.
China -said to have sold in to Tuesday's rally- has output costs around $1,075-$1,100 per tonne, Brandeis's Bahr said.
And he agreed that quite of lot of Chinese selling is likely to come in if LME cash prices get up to $1,140/50.
"But I don't think the Chinese are going to swamp the market. They'll sell a bit then allow the market to continue to rise," he added.
Chartists say $1,123/25 is a key resistance area, marking the top end of a sideways range the market has held since falling from a $1,239 high in January 1995.
